Email Personalisation Barriers in Automation 2026

By Emmanuel Obiechie · BuzzBurst Media · 8 min read

In 2026, nearly every email marketing platform promises "powerful personalisation." But walk behind the curtain of most UK startup campaigns and what you'll actually find is the same batch-and-blast approach that was already tired in 2019 — just with a first name in the subject line.

The problem isn't the tools. The problem is how brands are using them. Here's what's actually holding back email personalisation — and what ambitious UK brands should be doing instead.

1. Data poverty disguised as segmentation

Most email lists are built on two fields: first name and email address. That's not segmentation — that's a contact list. True personalisation requires behavioural data: what pages someone visited, what they clicked, how long they spent reading, what they bought or abandoned. Without this, "personalisation" is just cosmetic.

What to do: Before touching your automation platform, audit your data collection. Are you tracking on-site behaviour? Do you have post-purchase tags? Are your forms capturing intent signals beyond contact info?

2. Automation sequences built for the average customer

The "welcome sequence → nurture sequence → promotional sequence" framework was designed for the median subscriber. But your audience isn't median — it's individuals with different pain points, buying stages and timelines. Building one journey for everyone is the automation equivalent of one-size-fits-all clothing.

What to do: Map out at least 3 distinct subscriber personas and build branching journeys for each. Use conditional logic — most platforms support it. A startup founder who signed up from a GEO article should not receive the same sequence as a marketing manager who found you through paid ads.

3. Copy that sounds like it was written by a committee

Automated email copy tends to be safe, corporate and deliberately inoffensive. That's exactly why it doesn't convert. The irony is that personalisation at the copy level — writing with a specific person in mind, using their language, referencing their problem directly — drives more engagement than any dynamic content block.

What to do: Write each sequence as if you're writing to one specific person. Read it aloud. If it sounds like a press release, rewrite it until it sounds like a message.

4. Ignoring send-time optimisation

Sending at 10am Tuesday because "studies say so" is 2018 thinking. In 2026, send-time optimisation should be handled per-subscriber based on their historical open behaviour. Most enterprise platforms now offer this — yet most brands leave it disabled.

What to do: Enable per-subscriber send-time optimisation if your platform supports it. If not, A/B test send times across your segments quarterly and update accordingly.

The bottom line

Personalisation in 2026 is not a feature you switch on — it's a strategy you build. The brands winning in email marketing aren't the ones with the most sophisticated tech stack. They're the ones who understand their subscribers well enough to make every email feel like it was written for one person.

At BuzzBurst Media, we build email systems that are genuinely personal. If your email marketing feels generic, let's talk.
